passage: Sonali, you asked why I haven't switched to design yet. Honestly? It's the three years. I'm Mehak, third-year law, and I knew by the end of first year it wasn't for me. The case readings feel like chewing paper. But every time I open the design course page, I think: three years of fees, three years of Papa telling relatives "my daughter the lawyer", three years of my life. If I leave now, what were they for? So I just keep going. Some nights I sketch until two in the morning, and those are the only hours I feel awake. Then the alarm rings for moot court, and I tell myself, just two more years. Two more years so the first three aren't wasted.

qa.q: What year of law is Mehak in?
qa.a: Mehak is in third-year law.

qa.q: Why does Mehak keep going even though she knew in first year that law wasn't for her?
qa.a: Leaving would make the three years of fees, pride and effort feel wasted, so she keeps adding time to protect the time already spent.

qa.q: What question could help Mehak decide?
qa.a: She could ask which path she would choose if she were starting fresh today; the three years can't be recovered, but the next two can still be chosen.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel hearing about the sketching nights?
qa.a: Sonali may feel sad and concerned, noticing that the only hours Mehak feels awake are spent on design. 🤍

grounding: Shows a student staying in a degree that no longer fits because leaving would make the earlier years feel wasted.

passage: I'm Uma, and I've been Pankaj's friend since school. He's been with Ritika for four years now, since the first year of college. For the past year, every time I see them together, they seem to be arguing about small things: where to eat, who forgot to call. He told me once, "We want different lives, honestly. She wants to settle abroad, and I want to stay near my parents." But when I asked why he stays, he said, "Four years, Uma. Everyone knows us as a couple. How do I throw that away?" Last week he cancelled his own job interview in Pune because it would upset her plans. I don't know what he really feels. But he doesn't look happy.

qa.q: How long has Pankaj been with Ritika?
qa.a: Pankaj has been with Ritika for four years.

qa.q: What does Pankaj's question, "How do I throw that away?", show about his thinking?
qa.a: It shows Pankaj is afraid of wasting the four years and of what everyone would think, so the past matters more to him than whether the relationship fits his future.

qa.q: What could Uma gently ask Pankaj?
qa.a: Uma could ask what he would choose if he were meeting Ritika today, knowing what each of them wants now, and remind him the past four years still count even if the future changes.

qa.q: How might Ritika be affected if Pankaj stays only because of the four years?
qa.a: Ritika might end up with someone who is quietly unhappy and holding back his own plans, which is unfair to both of them.

grounding: Shows a young man staying in a relationship that no longer fits because leaving would make the four years feel wasted, as seen by a friend.

passage:
September: Jahnavi sat through another circuits lecture, drawing tiny portraits in the margins of her notes. Rafiq, her lab partner, asked why she didn't switch to the fine arts college. "Two years already," she said. "I can't just throw that away."
October: She failed the circuits mid-term. At the canteen she told Rafiq, "If I leave now, Papa's loan and my two years are all wasted." She looked tired.
December: After her portraits sold out at the college fair, Rafiq asked again. This time Jahnavi was quiet for a long while. "The two years are gone either way, aren't they?" she said. "I just don't want to lose the next four too." She booked a meeting with the college counsellor for Monday.

qa.q: What happened at the college fair in December?
qa.a: Jahnavi's portraits sold out at the college fair.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi's line about the next four years show about her feelings?
qa.a: It shows she has started to see that the two years can't be recovered, and she now fears losing future years more than wasting past ones.

qa.q: Why is booking the counsellor a good next step for Jahnavi?
qa.a: It lets her look at real options, like switching and handling the loan, with someone who can help, instead of deciding out of guilt about the past.

qa.q: How has Rafiq been part of Jahnavi's change?
qa.a: Rafiq kept asking the same kind question without pushing, which gave Jahnavi space to see the choice for herself.

grounding: Shows a student staying in a degree that doesn't fit because of the years already spent, and slowly seeing that the future can still be chosen.

passage: Kashish, you keep saying you can't break up because you've been together three years. Let your Avni masi tell you something. When I was twenty, in Indore, I had a boyfriend from my college. For the first year it was lovely. By the third year, we barely talked. He'd cancel plans, I'd cry, we'd make up, same thing again. My friends asked why I stayed. I said, "Three years! I can't just throw that away." It felt like leaving would make all those years a mistake. So I stayed one more year. Then one day, sitting alone in a café where he didn't show up again, I thought: the three years happened. They're mine. Staying won't make them better. It only takes the fourth. I ended it the next week. It hurt. But masi was free by twenty-one. So think about the next year, beta, not only the last three.

qa.q: How old was Avni masi when she ended the relationship?
qa.a: Masi was free by twenty-one.

qa.q: Why did young Avni stay in the relationship even after it stopped working?
qa.a: Avni was afraid that leaving would turn three years into a mistake, so staying seemed to protect the past, even though it cost her another year.

qa.q: What was Avni's turning point, and what did she decide?
qa.a: Sitting alone in the café when he didn't show up, she realised the past years were already hers and staying only takes more. She ended it the next week.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel hearing this story from Avni masi?
qa.a: Kashish may feel understood and less guilty about wanting to leave, and may start thinking about the next year instead of the last three.

grounding: An aunt tells Kashish how she once stayed in a failing relationship because leaving felt like wasting the years already spent.

passage: The transfer window at the university office closed at four, and at 3:10 the queue still stretched down the corridor. Ankita held two forms: one to stay in third-year architecture, one to switch to the psychology course she'd been sneaking into for months. Her friend Francis stood beside her, holding her bag. "You've filled both," he said. "Which one?" "I should stay. Two whole years. All those models, those nights. If I leave, it's all for nothing." "Do you like architecture?" She looked at the floor. "Not since first year." The queue shuffled forward. 3:35. "If you were starting today," Francis said, "which form would you pick?" Ankita didn't answer for a while. "Psychology," she whispered. "The two years still taught you things. They're not nothing." At 3:52 she reached the window and handed over the psychology form, her hands shaking.

qa.q: What time did the transfer window close?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: Why does Ankita feel she should stay in architecture?
qa.a: The two years of models and late nights feel like they would become worthless if she left. Staying feels like a way to honour that effort.

qa.q: What question helped Ankita choose, and why did it work under time pressure?
qa.a: "If you were starting today, which form would you pick?" It cut through the past and made her face what she wants now, so she handed in the psychology form.

qa.q: How might Francis feel as he watches Ankita hand in the form?
qa.a: He is probably relieved and proud of her, while understanding why her hands are shaking. 🙂

grounding: A student almost stays in a degree she no longer likes because of the years spent, and switches just before the deadline.

passage:
Monday. At Sahil's cousin's engagement, Rajni smiled for photos and felt nothing. They had been together since first year: three years, two anniversaries at the same café, his family already calling her "bahu" as a joke. They hardly talked any more except about exams.
Thursday. Her roommate asked, "Are you happy?" Rajni laughed. "That's not the point. Three years! If I end it now, what were those years for?" She lay awake counting everything she had given: birthdays, Sundays, the trip she skipped for him.
Sunday. On the college steps, Rajni wrote in her notebook: "The three years happened. They were good for a while. They stay good even if I leave." Under it she wrote: "Would I start this today?" She looked at the question for a long time before she called Sahil to ask if they could talk.

qa.q: How long had Rajni and Sahil been together?
qa.a: Since first year: three years.

qa.q: Why did Rajni laugh when asked if she was happy?
qa.a: She felt trapped and uneasy, because admitting unhappiness would make the three years feel wasted, so she brushed the question off.

qa.q: What question does Rajni finally ask herself, and why does it help?
qa.a: "Would I start this today?", which turns her toward the future she can still choose rather than the years she can't get back.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel when Rajni asks to talk?
qa.a: He may feel nervous or surprised, since they hardly talk now except about exams.

grounding: Over a week, a student stays in a relationship that no longer fits because leaving would make three years feel wasted, then starts to look forward.

passage: Karthik, you say you can't leave engineering because you've done two years. Listen to your Zeenat aunty for a minute. At nineteen I started a pharmacy degree because my father liked the idea. By second year I knew I hated it; I was happiest editing the college magazine. But I thought, two years, all those fees, all those nights. So I stayed. Third year, fourth year. I passed, just, and worked in a medicine shop for a year feeling like a ghost. At twenty-three I finally started journalism, older than everyone in my class. The two extra years didn't save the first two. They only added two more I didn't want. The day I left, I cried, and then I slept better than I had in years.

qa.q: What was young Zeenat happiest doing in college?
qa.a: Editing the college magazine.

qa.q: Why did young Zeenat stay in the pharmacy degree?
qa.a: She felt she couldn't waste two years of fees and nights, so the fear of losing them outweighed how unhappy she was.

qa.q: Which choice in the story could have come earlier, and what might have helped?
qa.a: Leaving after second year; asking whether she would start the degree today could have shown that the extra years wouldn't rescue the first two.

qa.q: How might Zeenat's father have felt about her staying in pharmacy?
qa.a: He was probably pleased, since he liked the idea, and may not have known how unhappy she was.

grounding: An aunt recalls staying in a degree she hated because leaving would make the first years feel wasted, only to lose two more.

passage: The course-change window closed at five, and it was already 3:40. Irfan sat outside the registrar's office with the form half filled: from B.Com to B.A. Psychology. He had spent the whole year dozing through accounts and reading psychology books under the desk. "Just sign it," said Ayesha, who had come with him for courage. Irfan's pen hovered. "One full year of B.Com, Ayesha. The fees, the books, the coaching Ammi paid for. If I switch, it's all gone." "It's gone anyway," she said gently. "The question is the next two years." The clock above the door said 4:52. Irfan looked at the form, then at the clock, and his hand shook. At 4:58 the clerk reached for the shutter.

qa.q: What course did Irfan want to switch to?
qa.a: B.A. Psychology.

qa.q: Why did Irfan's pen hover over the form?
qa.a: He felt torn and afraid that switching would make the year of fees, books and coaching feel wasted, even though he disliked B.Com.

qa.q: What would you advise Irfan in those last minutes?
qa.a: Focus on Ayesha's question about the next two years: the first year is spent either way, so choose the course he wants to keep studying.

qa.q: What is it like for Ayesha to watch the clock?
qa.a: Ayesha is probably anxious and a little frustrated, having come to give courage and seeing Irfan freeze as the deadline nears.

grounding: With a deadline closing, a student hesitates to leave a degree that no longer fits because the first year would feel wasted.

passage: Anirban was in the third year of mechanical engineering in Pune, and he hated it. Not the college, not his friends, just the subject. He spent lectures sketching characters for comics. His friend Rekha had seen his drawings and said more than once, "You should do animation. You're really good." Anirban always said the same thing: "I've done three years. If I leave now, it's three years wasted." So he went to lectures, failed a subject, took the re-exam, passed barely. At night, he drew until two. One evening Rekha showed him an animation course starting in June. He looked at the form a long time. Then he pushed it back. "Just one more year. Then I'll have a degree at least." He said it like a promise, but his voice was flat.

qa.q: What did Anirban sketch during lectures?
qa.a: Characters for comics.

qa.q: Why does Anirban keep studying engineering despite hating it?
qa.a: Leaving feels like making three years wasted, so the past years feel like a reason to continue even though he's unhappy and flat.

qa.q: What could Anirban ask himself to decide more freely?
qa.a: He could ask whether he'd choose engineering today knowing what he knows, and talk to a career counsellor about animation.

qa.q: How does Rekha seem to feel about Anirban's choice?
qa.a: Rekha seems encouraging but a little frustrated, seeing his talent and hoping he'll choose it.

grounding: It shows a student who stays in a degree that no longer fits because leaving would make earlier years feel wasted.

"Gopika, you've been crying again."
"It's nothing, Seema."
"It's Rahul, isn't it?"
"We had the same fight. Again."

"Four years, Seema. Four years. We've been together since first year. If I leave now, what was all that for?"
"It was for those four years. They happened. They're not going anywhere."
"It feels like throwing them away."
"You're not throwing them away. You're choosing the next four."
Gopika wiped her eyes, but shook her head. "I can't. Not yet."

passage: I spent three years preparing for the chartered accountancy exams. Three years of evening classes, mock papers, early mornings. By the second year, I knew it wasn't for me. I loved teaching; I helped my cousins with maths every weekend and came alive. But every time I thought of stopping, I felt sick. All those years. All that effort. I'd be admitting I'd wasted them. My friend Dilnaz asked once, "Sarita, if you were starting today, would you pick CA?" I said no immediately. Then I said, "But I didn't start today." I stayed another year. I failed the intermediate exam again. Looking back, I think I kept going to protect my past, not my future. This year I finally applied for a B.Ed. I'm still sad about the lost years. But I'm not losing more.

qa.q: What did Sarita finally apply for this year?
qa.a: A B.Ed.

qa.q: Why did Sarita stay in CA preparation for another year?
qa.a: Stopping felt like admitting the years were wasted, which made Sarita feel sick, so the past effort felt like a reason to continue.

qa.q: What helped Sarita finally change course?
qa.a: Seeing that staying protected the past, not the future, and choosing teaching based on what Sarita loves now.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when Sarita said 'But I didn't start today'?
qa.a: Dilnaz may have felt frustrated and sad, seeing Sarita stuck despite knowing the answer.

grounding: It shows a student who stayed in a path that no longer fit because leaving would make earlier years feel wasted, before finally choosing the future.

passage:
College counsellor's note

Parveen, third-year mechanical engineering, came in today. She said she's been unhappy in the course since first year. She wants to study psychology. She's been reading about it in her free time for two years.

When I asked why she hasn't switched, she said, "If I leave now, three years are wasted. My parents will think I threw it all away. I'd be starting over at twenty-one."

I listened. Then I asked her to imagine two versions of herself at twenty-five: one who finished engineering and is still unhappy, and one who switched. She was quiet for a while. She said the second one sounded lighter.

We talked about how the three years aren't erased: she learned maths, problem-solving and persistence.

She's going to talk to her parents this weekend and look at bridging courses. I'll see her again next week.

Hansa

qa.q: What does Parveen want to study instead?
qa.a: She wants to study psychology.

qa.q: Why has Parveen stayed in engineering even though she's unhappy?
qa.a: Parveen feels afraid that leaving would waste three years and disappoint her parents, so staying feels safer.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that helped Parveen think about the future?
qa.a: Hansa asked Parveen to imagine two versions of herself at twenty-five, helping her see the future can still be chosen.

qa.q: How might Parveen's parents react to the conversation this weekend?
qa.a: Parveen's parents may feel worried about the years spent at first but, if they listen, may be relieved she's finding a clearer path.

grounding: A counsellor notes a student who stays in a degree she dislikes because leaving would make three years feel wasted.

passage:
Sunday night

Tashi and I have been together since first year. Three years. Everyone thinks we're perfect. And I'm not happy. I haven't been for months.

We don't talk anymore. We just sit together on our phones. When I told Hafsa, she asked, "Why are you still in it?"

I said, "Three years, Hafsa. I've put so much into this. If I leave, it's all for nothing."

She said something I keep thinking about. "The three years happened. They were real. Leaving won't erase them. But staying won't bring them back either."

I think I've been staying because leaving feels like admitting I wasted my time. But I don't want to spend another three years like this.

I'm going to talk to Tashi this week. Kindly. Honestly.

Pema

qa.q: How long have Pema and Tashi been together?
qa.a: Since first year. Three years.

qa.q: Why has Pema stayed in the relationship despite being unhappy?
qa.a: Pema feels afraid that leaving would make the three years feel wasted, like admitting the time was lost.

qa.q: What did Hafsa say that helped Pema see things differently?
qa.a: Hafsa said the three years were real and leaving won't erase them, but staying won't bring them back either.

qa.q: How might Tashi feel when Pema talks to them this week?
qa.a: Tashi may feel hurt and surprised, or perhaps relieved if they have also been unhappy.

grounding: A student stays in a relationship that no longer fits because leaving would make three years feel wasted.

passage: During the Sankranti break, the fields around Kondapur were stubble and kite string. Raghav spent the whole morning under the old water pump behind the temple, and by noon it was running again. Anjali, who studied at the same town college, watched him wipe grease off his hands. "You look happier now than in two years of accounts class," she said. "I'm leaving B.Com after this semester. I've got a seat in the ITI electrical course." Raghav laughed too loudly. "And throw away two years? Amma sold her gold earrings for my first fee." "Those years are spent either way." He looked at the humming pump, then down the road to the bus stand where the college bus would leave on Monday. "If I leave now, it means everything was a waste," he said, and walked home to find his ledger notebooks.

qa.q: What did Raghav repair during the Sankranti break?
qa.a: He repaired the old water pump behind the temple.

qa.q: Why does leaving B.Com feel so hard for Raghav?
qa.a: He feels guilty and scared that leaving would make the two years, and Amma's gold earrings, feel wasted, so staying seems like the loyal choice.

qa.q: What question could help Raghav decide more fairly?
